newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac seeks to revive election campaign.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac seeks to revive election campaign.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac appealed on Tuesday for French voters to back his centre-right coalition in a snap parliamentary election as a new poll showed most people were disappointed with his record as head of state.

The appeal in a newspaper article, seen as an effort to breathe new life into the government's lacklustre election campaign, was to appear on Wednesday in 14 regional dailies from Lille in the north to Nice in the south.

The appeal, timed to coincide with the second anniversary of his election as president, was to appear as a new round of polls showed the centre-right's lead in the race for the May 25-June 1 National Assembly elections had all but evaporated.
"Things are open. The movement is even a little bit in our favour," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said on a trip to Brittany.
A Sofres poll published in the daily Le Monde said 65 percent of 1,000 people questioned were disappointed by Chirac's policies since he was elected two years ago.
A CSA survey saw the centre-right keeping power but with a sharply reduced majority of 296 seats to 258 for the combined left in the National Assembly.

The Sofres poll said Chirac, who dissolved parliament and called the election nine months ahead of schedule, was most harshly judged on his record in the fight against unemployment and social inequalities -- the two issues seen in earlier polls as the voters' top two concerns.
Of the seven issues surveyed, European policy was the only one on which Chirac scored positive marks: 45 percent of voters were satisfied against 34 percent who were dissatisfied.

Highlighting Chirac's gamble in calling the snap election, a BVA poll for the weekly Paris Match said 50 percent of voters wanted Chirac to stay on if the left won but a significant 41 percent believed he should quit.
A CSA poll for the weekly L'Evenement du Jeudi said 55 percent wanted him to stay on and work with a left-wing prime minister, as against 33 percent who said he should resign.

"Nobody doubts Chirac will vote RPR," said Daniel Vaillant, the Socialists' number two, referring to the Gaullist Rally for the Republic party founded by Chirac and now led by Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
"If Mr Juppe is calling for help from Mr Chirac, it means his campaign isn't going very well," Vaillant said.

Many politicians said Chirac needed to explain more clearly his decision to call the election almost 10 months early. He has said France needs a new impulse, partly to help it join a single European currency from a position of strength.

But the election has allowed the left and far right to accuse Chirac of having a secret agenda of unpopular austerity measures to help qualify for European monetary union from 1999, or of wanting to pre-empt emerging sleaze scandals.
Chirac, elected to a seven-year term in 1995, is meant to be above day-to-day politics, but presidents often seek to use their prestige to sway voters behind their allies.
However, Chirac could end up as a virtual lame duck for five years if voters ignore his advice and elect the opposition.
